subject: Civil Engineering
title: Corrosion: The Silent Destroyer
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Corrosion: The Silent Destroyer.

hook.text: The Champlain Towers collapsed in 2021. Years of hidden corrosion ate the rebar.

buildup.text: Salt water seeps into cracks, reaches steel reinforcement, and starts rusting.

discovery.text: Rust expands to eight times steel's volume, cracking the concrete from inside.

twist.text: External paint looks fine. The damage hides inside where nobody can see it.

climax.text: Cathodic protection and epoxy-coated rebar slow corrosion, but inspection is key.

punchline.text: Rust never sleeps, and neither should inspectors.

quiz.question: How does corrosion damage reinforced concrete from within?
options: Rust dissolves the concrete around the steel bars
Rust expands to many times steel's volume, cracking the concrete outward
Corroded steel becomes magnetic and repels the concrete

details.summary: Corrosion is the electrochemical deterioration of metals exposed to moisture and oxygen, converting structural steel back to iron oxide at a rate that can destroy structural capacity over decades.
details.whyItMatters: Corrosion is the single largest cause of structural deterioration worldwide, costing hundreds of billions of dollars annually in repairs and replacements of bridges, buildings, and infrastructure.
takeaways: Corrosion requires moisture, oxygen, and often chlorides or carbonation to proceed
Steel volume increases several times when it corrodes, fracturing concrete cover
Protective strategies include coatings, cathodic protection, and corrosion-resistant alloys

faq.question: How does corrosion damage reinforced concrete structures?
faq.answer: When reinforcing steel corrodes, it expands to about six times its original volume. This expansion creates enormous pressure inside the concrete, cracking and eventually spalling the cover. Exposed steel corrodes faster, accelerating deterioration in a vicious cycle.

faq.question: What methods prevent or slow corrosion in new structures?
faq.answer: Adequate concrete cover thickness and low-permeability concrete mix designs slow chloride penetration. Epoxy-coated or galvanized rebar adds physical barriers. Stainless steel rebar eliminates the corrosion risk entirely in critical applications.
